title: Your service

segments.voice: Yesterday, your neighbor. Your line: start next door. Did you learn a name, or use one you already knew? Next door is where it starts. Today, how far it can go. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

Son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says Allah will speak words like these on the Day of Resurrection. The person is bewildered. How could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And the answer comes: My servant so-and-so was sick, and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. The same exchange follows about food and about water. A hospital room, a hungry stranger, a thirsty one. Today, serving people as worship. Khidmah.
screen: `I WAS SICK.` → `HOW COULD I VISIT YOU?` → `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Khidmah is service, the work of looking after someone else's needs. In Muslim communities you'll hear it used for everything from serving tea at a gathering to running a food pantry. Next, why service counts as worship. That hadith does something bold. It doesn't put service next to worship. It puts Allah inside the visit. Nobody in the story is praying, and yet the sick room is where Allah is found. Third, how it's meant to be done. In surah al-Insan, the Qur'an describes people who give food, for love of Him, to the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and who say: we feed you only for the sake of Allah; we want no reward from you and no thanks. No reward and no thanks. That is a high bar, and an honest one. Service that waits for applause starts to become about the server. Then the intention behind it. The same hour at a shelter can be a chore, a line on an application, or worship. The givers in al-Insan say theirs out loud: for the sake of Allah. What changes is what the hour is for. Last, the promise. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says Allah is in the help of His servant as long as the servant is in the help of his brother. So service isn't only something given away. In the tradition's telling, the one who serves is also being served.
screen: `KHIDMAH: LOOKING AFTER NEEDS.` · `ALLAH FOUND IN THE SICK ROOM.` · `NO REWARD, NO THANKS.` · `HELPED WHILE HELPING.`

segments.voice: The practice: volunteer once. For now, sit and breathe. Let your breath go out a little longer than it comes in. Bring to mind someone who is sick, or alone, or short of something this week. Someone real, if you can. Hold them in mind, gently, without trying to fix anything yet. Then let the hadith's question land: if you visited, what would you find there? Now think of one place near you where people serve: a shelter, a food bank, a hospital, a mosque kitchen, an older neighbor's yard. If you pray, you can make your intention for Allah before you go. If you don't, simply set your intention to show up without needing thanks. After the bell, sign up for one shift, or make one visit. The bell holds the time.
Khidmah. Service to people, given for Allah's sake, without waiting for reward or thanks. Today's word.
Your line: serve. Today, do one helpful thing for someone who can't thank you, and don't tell anyone about it. Tomorrow, your balance. Day one thousand four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Muslims serve others through food pantries, hospital visits, mosque kitchens and community volunteering, describing it as khidmah, service, and as worship when done for Allah's sake; a hadith says that whoever visits the sick will find Allah there.

trapdoor: what you thought: volunteering is a nice extra, separate from religion.
what it means: khidmah, service to people, counted as worship when it's done for Allah without waiting for thanks.
what a scholar hears: the hadith qudsi of the sick visit, al-Insan's 'no reward, no thanks', and Allah's help for the one who helps.
